posts.image_prompt: A heavy weathered grey stone slab lying among the tangled roots of a freshly uprooted tree on a late-1890s Minnesota farm field, faint carved marks on its face, a farmer in overalls looking down at it, autumn light
posts.caption:
🪨 DID VIKINGS REACH MINNESOTA IN 1362?

In 1898, Swedish immigrant farmer Olof Ohman was clearing trees on his land near Kensington, Minnesota. Tangled in the roots, he said, was a stone slab carved with runes.

The inscription claimed that a party of Swedes and Norwegians had travelled there in 1362 and suffered a tragedy.

If real, it would rewrite American history. It was even displayed at the Smithsonian in 1948–49.

But experts who studied the runes in 1899 found too many oddities in form and vocabulary for 14th-century Scandinavian. Most scholars since have agreed. In 1958, scholar Erik Wahlgren concluded it was a deliberate fraud, and in 1974 a confession by a local man, John Gran, to his children came to light, saying it was carved as a joke.

Today it sits in a museum in Alexandria, Minnesota — and still has believers.

Why do you think hoaxes like this are so hard to kill?

Hero of Alexandria described a coin-operated dispenser for temples: the coin's weight tipped a lever that briefly opened the flow.

posts.topic: Cahokia, the city of the mounds
posts.image_prompt: A vast ancient Native American city at sunrise with a huge terraced earthen mound topped by a large thatched wooden building, smaller mounds and thatched houses spreading across a river floodplain, smoke from cooking fires, cinematic wide aerial view
posts.caption:
🏞️ NORTH AMERICA'S FORGOTTEN CITY

Near modern St. Louis, Illinois, lie the remains of Cahokia — once the largest Native American city north of Mexico.

People settled here around 600 AD. From the 9th century they began building huge earthen mounds. At least 120 once stood here, and about 80 survive today.

The largest, Monks Mound, rises in terraces and was the city's focal point.

How many people lived here at its height? Estimates vary widely — from around 15,000 in the central city to as many as 40,000 by some counts. By some estimates, that rivaled London at the time.

Then, by around 1350, the city was abandoned. Researchers suggest drought or floods, political turmoil, or strain on food supplies. Nobody knows for sure.

Why do you think Cahokia isn't better known?

posts.title: 129 men vanished in the Arctic

scenes.image_prompt: Two wooden 19th-century Royal Navy ships trapped in thick sea ice under a pale Arctic sky, masts frosted, vast white emptiness
scenes.narration: In 1845, two British ships sailed into the Arctic and vanished.
scenes.image_search: HMS Erebus HMS Terror in the ice

scenes.image_prompt: Two sailing ships departing an English harbour in 1845, crowds waving from the dock, flags flying
scenes.narration: Sir John Franklin led one hundred and twenty-nine men on HMS Erebus and HMS Terror to find the Northwest Passage.
scenes.label: 129 MEN

scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of an old handwritten note on weathered paper inside a tin cylinder, set on Arctic stones
scenes.narration: Years later, searchers found a note in a stone cairn. The first message said, all well. A second one, added in 1848, did not.

scenes.image_prompt: Sailors in heavy wool coats pulling sledges across endless sea ice, abandoned ships in the far distance
scenes.narration: Franklin had died in 1847. The ships were trapped in ice and abandoned. One hundred and five survivors set off on foot.

scenes.image_prompt: A Victorian gentleman reading a newspaper in a London club, shocked expression, gaslight, 1854
scenes.narration: On October 23, 1854, The Times reported explorer John Rae's grim news: the men had died. Britain was stunned.

scenes.image_prompt: Dozens of search ships and sledge teams spread across Arctic ice and islands, map-like wide view
scenes.narration: More than thirty search expeditions went looking. The ships stayed lost.

scenes.image_prompt: An underwater view of a wooden shipwreck on the seabed in green Arctic water, a ship's bell visible, divers' lights
scenes.narration: Until the twist. Erebus was found in 2014, Terror in 2016. Both sitting on the Arctic seabed.

scenes.image_prompt: An empty Arctic shoreline with a lone stone cairn at sunset, ice floes drifting
scenes.narration: What should explorers search for next? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🧊 ON THIS DAY in 1854, The Times carried explorer John Rae's report on the fate of the lost Franklin Expedition.

In 1845, 129 men sailed for the Arctic on HMS Erebus and HMS Terror and never came home. A note left in a cairn in 1848 said the ships had been abandoned in the ice and Franklin was already dead.

More than 30 search expeditions failed to find the ships. Then Erebus was discovered in 2014 and Terror in 2016.

We still don't fully know how the men died. What do you think went wrong? 👇
